messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm using a community model to investigate the relationship between occupancy of prairie-associated reptile and amphibian assemblages and some habitat/landscape covariates, and I have a conceptual question related to this. We're dealing with a tricky scenario where we failed to document some rare species at particular sites during our formal surveys, but they were haphazardly documented (either by us or by other trusted observers) at those sites during the study period. We'd like to incorporate those known presences to better inform our occupancy relationships, and I'm struggling to find a way to explicitly build that into the model. Does anyone have ideas/experience doing that, or, given that we're primarily interested in occupancy and not detection, should we simply count those outside detections as survey detections?

Thanks in advance for any advice,

Ethan Royal

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ethan,

I would believe that there are multiple ways of doing this, assuming you're using some BUGS software. One would be to simply declare the presence/absence state of those sites known. I.e. taking them out of the part of the model that goes like this:   z[i] ~ dbern(psi)

Instead for them you write this:    z[i] <- 1

I believe that another method might be to add these '1's' in a sort of special occasion in the detection history matrix, then not change anything in the model for the z's, but instead estimating a fully separate value of detection probability exclusively for this single occasion. This parameter would then not be estimable, and you wouldn't want to estimate it, but in this way you would still incorporate the information about the presences into the model. This method would probably also work with unmarked.

I'd be interested in whether others think that something in these ideas is wrong.

Best regards -- Marc

Hi guys, I agree with Marc about the second strategy.

I dabbled with this in a mark-recapture context, for example when known radio-tagged individuals were uncaptured during a sampling period.  What I did was include a separate likelihood to estimate a probability ("p.known") of being tagged, with an individual's "tagged" status as an observation of a Bernoulli variable (0/1):

tagged[i] ~ dbern(p.known * z[i])

This allowed those individuals to have a known z state of 1, despite having an all-zero capture history.  The "p.known" parameter is the proportion of N that is tagged.  This construct seemed to work fine under various simulations we explored.

In an occupancy context, "p.known" would be the proportion of occupied sites for species X that had an ancillary presence observation.  Obviously this parameter does not have any value in and of itself and only serves to inform the z states.

Hi everyone, I am running a multi-state model of nest-cavity occupancy and doing imputation of unobserved states that enter the analysis as NA. Looking at the AHM1 book (page 174) I see interesting detail about imputation of covariate data. Does anyone know of an explanation that goes into comparable detail about imputation of unobserved states? I also wonder, just for curiosity, if this can only be done in the Bayesian context or if there are precedents of anything that looks like imputation of unobserved states in the maximum likelihood framework.

Maybe someone could recommend some reading?

I would greatly appreciate your help

Thank you

Hello,
If i understood correctly, when you talk about imputation and NA records I just think about missing data, which is a quiet sensible area of statistics.

When talking about missing data I use this book:
Molenberghs, G., & Kenward, M. (2007). Missing data in clinical studies (Vol. 61). John Wiley & Sons.

There is an advantage of using missing data in the Bayesian framework, and that is that the missing values are treat as any other parameters of the model. Therefore techniques as Data Augmentation are useful.
Having this in a likelihood framework may be hard, because of the structure of the missing data, there are three different types: "missing completely at random", "missing at random" and "missing not at random"
Depending on what you have you have, different techniques of likelihood are possible.

I hope this was of any help,
If i was not clear or I did not understood the question, just let me know :)

Have a nice day
--

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

it is our great pleasure to advertise the publication by Academic Press of our brand-new textbook on Integrated Population Models (IPMs), see cover attached. IPMs are an incredibly powerful framework for making the most of your data in population modeling, by fusing in a single statistical model multiple data sets on population counts and demographic quantities such as survival or productivity. In our book, we first give a comprehensive account of the theory of IPMs. In the second half, we then present a wide range of case studies that give a flavour of the tremendous power of these models to answer research questions and solve wildlife management problems. We provide vast amounts of very easily accessible code in R and JAGS, so we hope that the book, along with the associated resources, will kick-​start your own applications of IPMs.

You can get much more information on our book on the book website: www.vogelwarte.ch/ipm <http://www.vogelwarte.ch/ipm>. One of the bonus resources is a long document that you can download and which gives complete and richly commented code for the solutions to all the exercises in the book. In addition, you will find links to access all the code in the book on GitHub and to the R package IPMbook (available on CRAN), which contains useful functions and all data sets. Both the GitHub repo and the R package were created and are maintained by our colleague Mike Meredith (https://mmeredith.net/). Mike has been an invaluable help for the entire book project (see also book Acknowledgements) and is very warmly acknowledged.

Michael and Marc

Dear all,

I just started with nimble, converting my JAGS code to it. I am getting errors while compiling the model with the nimbleModel() function, but it doesn't give me any line numbers!  Like this:

"Defining model
Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames,  :
  Dynamic indexing found in a vector of indices, 1:k. Only scalar indices, such as 'idx' in 'x[idx]', can be dynamic. One can instead use dynamic indexing in a vector of indices inside a nimbleFunction."

How do I get nimble to tell me the line number in the model code where problem occurs? I cannot believe that such already famous software would just let you debug like this, because that's quite unusable.

Thanks a lot and best regards,

Tomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

Sorry to hear you're having a bumpy first experience using nimble.  Informative error-trapping can be difficult.  I understand your reaction.

There is a nimble-users list (information at https://r-nimble.org/more/issues-and-groups).  You can post there for more support.  You will likely be asked to share your code, on-list if you don't mind, off-list if you prefer.

What the error message is saying is that somewhere you have something like x[1:k] on the right-hand side of a model declaration (a line of model code), where k itself is declared as stochastic (meaning somewhere there is a "k ~ d<something>(...)".  Because nimble creates an internal representation of the graphical model relationships -- what depends on what -- a stochastically (aka dynamically) indexed vector is difficult to handle.   We say something is dynamically indexed if the index itself is a variable that might for example be sampled by MCMC.  Scalar dynamic indexing is easily supported, e.g. "y ~ dnorm(mu[k], sd = sigma)" where k is stochastic such as "k ~ dcat(probs[1:N])" so that k takes values in 1, 2, ... N.  The difficulty is vector dynamic indexing, like x[1:k].  The message is saying that a good way to accomplish that is by writing a nimbleFunction to use in the model, which simply means writing a function in a way that nimble can compile it.  For example, if you want

sum_x <- sum(x[1:k]) # where k is stochastic

you could instead do

sum_x <- dynamic_sum(x[1:N], start = 1, end = k) # where N is static (given in the `constants` [or `data`] lists) and is the maximum possible value of k.

dynamic_sum <- nimbleFunction(
 run = function(x = double(1), start = double(), end = double()) { # declares x is a vector and start and end are scalars.  All values in models are double precision even if only integers are needed.
   return(sum(x[start:end]))
   returnType(double()) # return will be scalar
 })

Now, in the graphical model, sum_x will depend on all of x[1:N] and on k, and the nimbleFunction that calculates sum_x will return sum(x[1:k]).

HTH
-Perry
